cultivar: Zijuan (purple-leaf cultivar selected from Yunnan large-leaf stock)
processing: Fully oxidised black tea from the anthocyanin-rich Zijuan cultivar: withered, rolled, oxidised and dried, usually with gentle heat so the purple pigments and fruit aroma survive.
harvest_season: Spring (March–April) gives the deepest colour and sweetest cup; summer leaf is more bitter.
appearance_dry: Slim, tightly twisted leaves in purple-black with a dull violet sheen and a few reddish tips.
appearance_liquor: Deep amber-red, at times with a faint violet cast in the first steeps.
appearance_wet: Purple-brown leaves with violet stems and veins.
taste_profile: Grape skin, plum and a rose-like floral over honey, with a tart, faintly bitter edge that keeps it lively rather than cloying.

brewing.notes: Cooler water (85–90 °C) and short steeps tame the anthocyanin bitterness; a squeeze of lemon turns the liquor pinker, a party trick that works because of the pigments.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring harvest, occasionally the previous one; it is pleasant for a year or two in a sealed bag and is not aged, unlike sheng made from the same cultivar.
description:
Zi Juan is Yunnan's purple tea cultivar, and Zi Juan black is the gentlest way to drink it. The cultivar goes back to purple-budded bushes found on Nanuo Mountain in Menghai in 1954; it was fixed as a clone at the Yunnan tea research institute in 1985, and it is purple all over – buds, leaves and stems – because it is unusually rich in anthocyanins, the pigments that colour blueberries and red cabbage.

Made as green or sheng, those pigments stay high and the cup opens with a slight bitterness. Full oxidation lowers the anthocyanins and changes the equation: the leaf is withered, rolled, oxidised and dried like any Dian Hong, and the result is milder and honeyed, with at most a hint of purple left in the liquor. Makers use gentle drying to preserve the fruit aroma.

In the cup expect grape and plum first, a rose-like floral note, honey underneath and a tart, lightly bitter finish that keeps it from being sweet-flat. Brew it cooler than a normal Dian Hong, around 85–90 °C, and keep the steeps short; too hot and the bitterness takes over. It also makes a pretty cold brew.

It is sold as the current spring harvest, mostly by Yunnan specialists, and it is a cultivar name, not a grade, so there is no ladder to climb. Do not confuse it with 'wild purple bud' (zi ya) teas, which are from naturally purplish wild or old trees rather than this cultivar and taste quite different. The giveaway for real Zi Juan is purple stems in the wet leaf.

It is a conversation tea: brew it in a glass pot for guests who have only met the cultivar's reputation, then pour them a straight Dian Hong to show what the cultivar changed.
sources_note: Cultivar origin: selected 1985 at the Tea Research Institute of the Yunnan Academy of Agricultural Sciences (Menghai), per Chinese cultivar registers; stated as 'mid-1980s' to be safe.
history:
Zi Juan is a modern cultivar with a clear record. In 1954 Zhou Pengju of the Yunnan tea research institute noticed purplish bushes in a population garden on Nanuo Mountain in Menghai. Later Wang Chaoji and Wang Ping found a plant with purple stems, leaves and buds in a garden derived from that stock, first calling it Zi Jian and then renaming it Zi Juan.

It became a clonal cultivar in 1985 and received plant variety protection in 2005. Anthocyanins are its selling point, and the pigment level is higher in green and sheng versions than in black.

The black tea is a later use of the cultivar, and when it was first made is not documented. Described as mild with a fairly strong honey aroma, it stays a niche speciality.
